title: DOH Jan + Feb 2024
des: DOH (HAAD) paediatrics recall, 31 January 2024 and February 2024

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought by his grandmother with fever of 37.8 °C. He is frightened of you and his clothes are dirty, but there are no bruises. His throat is mildly red. What is your action?
questions.a: Treat the infection and admit to explore the social concerns
questions.b: Treat the infection and discharge home with advice to the grandmother
questions.exp: A fearful, unkempt child brought by a non-parent raises concern about neglect. The recalled answer is to treat the minor infection and admit, which gives a safe place to take a full social history and involve the safeguarding team before discharge.

questions.question: A 2-year-old with hydrocephalus had his VP shunt revised 6 weeks ago. He now has vomiting and low-grade fever. He is sleepy but rousable, with no focal neurological deficit. What is your plan?
questions.a: Reassure and follow up after 3 days
questions.c: Admit and order an urgent CT head
questions.exp: Vomiting, fever and drowsiness within weeks of a shunt revision mean shunt malfunction or shunt infection until proven otherwise. Admit, request urgent neuroimaging (CT or rapid MRI, plus shunt series) and involve neurosurgery for a shunt tap.

questions.question: Which of the following is the LEAST common condition in preschool children?
questions.exp: Köhler disease (avascular necrosis of the navicular, usually boys aged 4–7) is rare. Physeal (Salter–Harris) fractures are common at every age, and systemic JIA peaks at 1–5 years. A fourth option beginning 'Oste…' was only partly recalled: if it was Osgood–Schlatter disease or osteosarcoma, those belong to adolescence and would be the better answer.

questions.question: What is a common cause of acute kidney injury in children?
questions.exp: HUS is the commonest cause of intrinsic (renal) AKI in young children. Note that dehydration from gastroenteritis is the commonest cause of pre-renal AKI overall, so read the exact wording; the recall gave HUS.

questions.question: At what developmental age (in months) does a baby smile, respond to his name and sit with a little support?
questions.exp: Sitting with support and turning to his own name fit about 6 months (social smile from 6 weeks; sitting without support around 7–8 months).

questions.question: A boy has recurrent sinopulmonary infections and a low platelet count with small platelets. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (X-linked, WAS gene): eczema, recurrent infections and thrombocytopenia with SMALL platelets. Bernard–Soulier has large platelets; ITP does not cause infections.

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy presents with a Salter–Harris fracture. What is your action?
questions.a: Admit, fix the fracture and investigate for child abuse
questions.b: Fix the fracture and discharge home
questions.exp: A fracture in a child under 2–3 years without a clear, consistent mechanism should prompt a safeguarding assessment (history, skeletal survey as indicated) alongside orthopaedic treatment.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with a limp. X-ray shows a flattened femoral epiphysis and a widened joint space. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Flattening and fragmentation of the femoral head with joint-space widening in a 4–8-year-old is Perthes disease. SUFE affects obese adolescents and shows posterior-inferior slip of the epiphysis. (The recall first marked SUFE and then corrected it to LCPD.)

questions.question: Same scenario (Perthes disease) in a 5-year-old. What is the management?
questions.a: Conservative: analgesia, physiotherapy and activity modification (± brace/splint)
questions.exp: Under about 6 years Perthes has a good prognosis and is managed conservatively to keep hip movement. Surgery (osteotomy) is for older children or poor containment. 'Surgical fixation' (pinning) is the treatment of SUFE. The recall marked surgical fixation, which looks like a mix-up with SUFE.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with a limp. X-ray shows a small femoral head and a widened joint space. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Small, dense or fragmented femoral head with joint-space widening = Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head).

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia presents with right hip pain and cannot bear weight. X-ray shows a small femoral head and a widened joint space. What is the diagnosis?
questions.b: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (Perthes-like)
questions.exp: The X-ray changes are those of avascular necrosis of the femoral head, a recognised complication of sickle cell disease that looks like Perthes. A simple vaso-occlusive crisis has a normal X-ray. The recall marked both Perthes and VOC.

questions.question: A child had a leg injury with a 10 cm wound. Three days later he has fever, a tender leg and restricted movement. You order an X-ray. What do you expect to see?
questions.a: No bony change yet; it is too early
questions.exp: In acute osteomyelitis plain X-ray changes (periosteal elevation, lytic areas) appear only after 10–14 days. MRI is the imaging of choice early on.

questions.question: A 3-month-old presents unconscious with multiple subdural haematomas; the picture suggests child abuse. What is your action?
questions.a: ICU admission, neurosurgical review, treat raised ICP and inform social services about suspected abuse
questions.b: ICU admission, skeletal survey and a child-protection meeting
questions.exp: Resuscitate and stabilise first: ICU, neurosurgery, measures to lower ICP, and a safeguarding referral. The skeletal survey, ophthalmology review and strategy meeting follow once the child is stable.

questions.question: In diabetic ketoacidosis, why is the fluid deficit corrected over 48 hours?
questions.a: To reduce the risk of cerebral oedema
questions.d: To avoid fluid overload and heart failure
questions.exp: Slow, even correction of the deficit over 48 hours (BSPED/ISPAD) is intended to limit rapid osmolality shifts that are linked to cerebral oedema.

questions.question: A child is newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes after presenting in DKA. Which is correct?
questions.a: Start a multiple daily injection (basal–bolus) insulin regimen from diagnosis
questions.b: Aim for an HbA1c above 6.5% (48 mmol/mol)
questions.exp: NICE recommends an MDI basal–bolus regimen (or pump) from diagnosis and an HbA1c target of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower.

questions.question: A neonate presents with bruises all over the body. Which question is most important to ask?
questions.b: Did he receive vitamin K at birth?
questions.c: What is the mother's blood group?
questions.exp: Bruising in a neonate suggests vitamin K deficiency bleeding; always ask whether vitamin K was given at birth (and check coagulation).

questions.question: A baby is born to a mother with hepatitis B. In which situation does the baby receive hepatitis B vaccine WITHOUT hepatitis B immunoglobulin?
questions.a: Mother HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive
questions.b: Mother HBsAg positive and anti-HBe positive (low viral load)
questions.c: Mother had acute hepatitis B during pregnancy
questions.d: Mother HBsAg positive with HBV DNA ≥ 10^6 IU/mL
questions.exp: HBIG is added for babies of mothers who are HBeAg positive, HBsAg positive without e-markers, have a high viral load, or had acute hepatitis B in pregnancy. A mother who is HBsAg positive but anti-HBe positive (low infectivity) needs the vaccine course only.

questions.question: Which vaccines are given at 8 weeks in the UK 2020 schedule?
questions.exp: From January 2020 the PCV dose at 8 weeks was dropped (PCV at 12 weeks and 1 year). The 8-week visit is 6-in-1, MenB and rotavirus. (The recall gave only the question; options are reconstructed.)

questions.question: A neonate has Erb's palsy. Which of the following is true?
questions.a: An associated clavicle fracture heals within about 3 weeks; the arm is followed up
questions.b: It results from injury to the C8–T1 roots
questions.d: Most babies need surgery in the first month
questions.exp: Erb's palsy is a C5–C6 injury (waiter's tip, intact grasp). A coexisting clavicle fracture is common and heals in 2–3 weeks; most palsies recover, with physiotherapy and follow-up. (Options reconstructed around the recalled answer.)

questions.question: Regarding Bell's palsy, which statement is NOT true?
questions.a: It can spare the upper face (forehead)
questions.b: Oral steroids within 72 hours improve recovery
questions.d: Eye protection is needed if the eye cannot close
questions.exp: Bell's palsy is a lower motor neurone lesion, so the forehead IS affected. Sparing of the forehead points to an upper motor neurone lesion.

questions.question: An HIV-positive mother started antiretroviral therapy at 15 weeks of pregnancy. What advice do you give to reduce transmission to her baby?
questions.exp: Avoiding breastfeeding removes postnatal transmission (BHIVA). Caesarean section is not needed when the viral load is suppressed (<50 copies/mL) at 36 weeks; the baby also gets post-exposure prophylaxis.

questions.question: A neonate with a positive family history of DDH is examined. The doctor adducts the hip and pushes the leg posteriorly. What is this manoeuvre?
questions.exp: Barlow: adduct and push backwards to dislocate an unstable hip. Ortolani: abduct and lift forwards to relocate a dislocated hip.

questions.question: A child has a heart rate of 270/min. Cardiac and other systemic examination are normal. What is your action?
questions.exp: A stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres first, then IV adenosine if they fail. Synchronised DC cardioversion is for the shocked child.

questions.question: A child with SLE presents with central chest pain. What do you suspect?
questions.exp: Serositis (pericarditis, pleuritis) is the commonest cardiac manifestation of SLE: central chest pain, better leaning forward.

questions.question: Which of the following reflects small airway obstruction?
questions.exp: Wheeze is mainly expiratory and comes from intrathoracic small airways; stridor is inspiratory and comes from the large extrathoracic airway.

questions.question: An infant presents with typical bronchiolitis. What is the management?
questions.a: Supportive: oxygen if saturation is low, and fluids/feeding support
questions.exp: NICE: bronchiolitis is managed supportively — oxygen if SpO2 is persistently below 90–92%, nasogastric or IV fluids if feeding is poor. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not recommended.

questions.question: A child has circumoral cyanosis, is pale, and has Hb 6 g/dL. What oxygen saturation would you expect?
questions.exp: Pulse oximetry measures the proportion of haemoglobin that is saturated, so anaemia itself does not lower SpO2. Circumoral blueness with pallor in anaemia is usually peripheral, and saturation is near normal (the recall gave 89%).

questions.question: A child is suspected of having bacterial meningitis. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: A normal CT excludes raised intracranial pressure, so LP is then safe
questions.b: CT is not reliable for excluding raised ICP; the decision to delay LP rests on clinical signs
questions.c: LP must be done before antibiotics in every case
questions.d: Dexamethasone is started 24 hours after antibiotics
questions.exp: NICE: do not rely on CT to decide whether LP is safe; delay LP for clinical signs of raised ICP, shock, coagulopathy or seizures. Antibiotics must not wait for LP; dexamethasone is given with or just before the first antibiotic dose. (The recall asked which is NOT true and gave this statement; options are reconstructed.)

questions.question: A child with chickenpox had high fever that settled 2 days ago, but the temperature is now 40 °C. If not treated, the child is at risk of which of the following?
questions.exp: A new fever after the initial fever of varicella settles suggests secondary bacterial infection, especially invasive group A streptococcus or staphylococcus, which can cause toxic shock syndrome and necrotising fasciitis.

questions.question: A child has periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis with normal vision and normal eye movements. Which investigation is needed?
questions.c: No imaging; it is a clinical diagnosis, treat and review
questions.d: CT of the orbit and sinuses
questions.exp: Preseptal cellulitis without orbital signs (normal acuity, colour vision, eye movements, no proptosis) needs no imaging. CT orbit and sinuses is reserved for suspected orbital involvement. The recall was unsure (X-ray sinus or MRI); neither is indicated.

questions.question: A child has orbital cellulitis with eye swelling, pain and visual disturbance. Which investigation is needed?
questions.a: Contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses
questions.exp: Visual disturbance, pain on eye movement, ophthalmoplegia or proptosis indicate orbital (post-septal) cellulitis: urgent contrast CT orbits, sinuses (± brain) to look for subperiosteal abscess, with IV antibiotics and ENT/ophthalmology review.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy presents with knee pain. He recently travelled to Finland and has a raised, spreading skin lesion. What is your management?
questions.exp: Erythema migrans with arthralgia after travel to a tick area = Lyme disease. NICE: doxycycline for children aged 9 and over; amoxicillin under 9; ceftriaxone for neurological or cardiac disease.

questions.question: A child is suspected of having retinoblastoma. Which investigation is appropriate?
questions.exp: Retinoblastoma is diagnosed by examination under anaesthesia with imaging (MRI of orbits and brain). Biopsy is avoided because of the risk of tumour seeding.

questions.question: In suspected coeliac disease, when is small bowel biopsy mandatory?
questions.a: When the child has IgA deficiency (low total IgA)
questions.b: When tTG-IgA is above 10× the upper limit and EMA is positive
questions.c: In any symptomatic child who is HLA-DQ2 positive
questions.d: To confirm response to a gluten-free diet
questions.exp: With low total IgA, IgA-based serology is unreliable; IgG-based tests are used and biopsy is required to confirm. ESPGHAN allows a no-biopsy diagnosis when tTG-IgA ≥10× ULN with positive EMA on a second sample.

questions.question: An 8-month-old has diarrhoea and weight loss since weaning, and anti-endomysial antibody is positive. What investigation do you order?
questions.exp: Coeliac screening is tTG-IgA together with total IgA, to make sure a negative or low result is not due to IgA deficiency.

questions.question: A 3-week-old neonate presents with stiffness, poor feeding and then seizures. There was prolonged rupture of membranes and the mother did not receive antibiotics. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Late-onset GBS disease (7 days to 3 months) typically presents as meningitis. Intrapartum antibiotics prevent early-onset but not late-onset disease.

questions.question: Regarding NICE guidance on urinary tract infection in children, which statement is NOT true?
questions.a: Infants under 3 months with suspected UTI should be referred to a paediatric specialist
questions.b: Dipstick testing is reliable in children over 3 years
questions.c: Every child with a first UTI needs a DMSA scan
questions.d: An infant under 6 months with atypical UTI needs ultrasound during the acute illness
questions.exp: NICE: DMSA 4–6 months after infection is for children under 3 with atypical or recurrent UTI, and older children with recurrent UTI, not for every first UTI. (The recall gave only the topic; options reconstructed.)

questions.question: Regarding renal imaging in children, which statement is correct?
questions.a: DMSA is the best test for renal scarring and is done 4–6 months after the infection
questions.b: MCUG is indicated for every child with a first UTI
questions.d: MAG3 is the first-line test for renal scarring
questions.exp: DMSA (static scan) shows cortical scarring; it is delayed 4–6 months so acute inflammation is not mistaken for scar. MCUG detects VUR and is reserved for selected infants. (Recall gave only the topic; options reconstructed.)

questions.question: A patient on cyclophosphamide presents with haematuria, proteinuria and positive nitrites. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acrolein, a cyclophosphamide metabolite, causes haemorrhagic cystitis; it is prevented with hydration and mesna. Always send a urine culture, as nitrites can reflect infection.

questions.question: An infant has abdominal pain, cramps and constipation since starting cow's milk formula. On examination there is an urticarial rash and swelling around the mouth, with no airway, breathing or circulation compromise. What is your action?
questions.b: Eliminate cow's milk from the mother's and child's diet
questions.exp: Urticaria and lip swelling without respiratory or circulatory involvement is not anaphylaxis, so adrenaline is not indicated; give an antihistamine if needed. For a formula-fed infant with cow's milk protein allergy, switch to an extensively hydrolysed formula. Maternal elimination applies only to breastfed infants. The recall marked IM adrenaline; choose it only if the stem describes airway, breathing or circulation problems.

questions.question: A child has itchy, scaly skin with scratch marks in the flexures. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Itchy, dry, scaly flexural eczema with excoriation is atopic dermatitis.

questions.question: Same scenario (atopic dermatitis). What is the management?
questions.exp: Emollients plus a mild (low-potency) topical corticosteroid for flares; stepped up to moderate potency if needed.

questions.question: A child with eczema develops painful blisters (punched-out erosions). What is the cause?
questions.exp: Eczema herpeticum: monomorphic punched-out erosions and vesicles on eczematous skin. It is an emergency — start aciclovir.

questions.question: In asthma, which of the following is NOT related to mortality?
questions.exp: Markers of fatal asthma include previous admissions or severe attacks, needing IV magnesium, and over-use of reliever (salbutamol). Inhaled steroids are protective; under-use, not over-use, is the risk.

questions.question: A child has had linear (whorled) lesions following Blaschko's lines since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti (X-linked dominant, NEMO/IKBKG; usually girls): vesicular → verrucous → hyperpigmented → atrophic stages along Blaschko's lines.

questions.question: A girl who has just started school has a round patch of hair loss on her scalp with black dots. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Black-dot tinea capitis (Trichophyton tonsurans): hairs broken at the scalp surface. Treat with oral antifungal (griseofulvin or terbinafine).

questions.question: A child had glandular fever 1–2 months ago and now complains of leg weakness, but examination is normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fatigue and subjective weakness after EBV with normal examination (normal reflexes and power) suggests post-viral/chronic fatigue. GBS has objective weakness and absent reflexes. (Formal CFS/ME diagnosis needs symptoms for 3 months.)

questions.question: A patient presents with fever, sore throat, lymph node enlargement and splenomegaly. Which investigation do you order?
questions.exp: Infectious mononucleosis: Monospot (or EBV serology, which is better in young children because Monospot is often negative under 4 years). The blood film shows atypical lymphocytes.

questions.question: A girl of normal weight has short stature, oedema of the hands and amenorrhoea. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Turner syndrome (45,X): short stature, lymphoedema of the hands and feet, primary amenorrhoea from ovarian failure. Confirm with karyotype.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy is short with normal growth hormone; his father is short. He does not accept his situation, wants to be like his peers and is unhappy. What is your action?
questions.a: A short course of low-dose testosterone (about 3 months) to start puberty
questions.c: Refer to an adolescent psychology clinic
questions.exp: Constitutional delay with psychosocial distress: a 3–6-month course of low-dose testosterone induces puberty and helps self-esteem without affecting final height. Psychological support is also worthwhile (the recall marked both a and c).

questions.question: A 2-day-old neonate has respiratory distress and a continuous murmur. What is your immediate action?
questions.exp: A haemodynamically significant PDA: first-line supportive care includes fluid restriction; then echocardiography and medical closure (ibuprofen, indomethacin or paracetamol) if needed.

questions.question: A 6-week-old infant has respiratory distress, tender hepatomegaly and a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that does not radiate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A large VSD presents with heart failure at 4–6 weeks, as pulmonary vascular resistance falls: pansystolic murmur at the LLSE, tachypnoea, hepatomegaly, poor feeding.

questions.question: In a child over 3 years, what is the approximate sensitivity of a urine dipstick positive for leucocyte esterase OR nitrite for diagnosing UTI?
questions.exp: Leucocyte esterase or nitrite positive has a sensitivity of about 90% (lower specificity). Nitrite alone is specific but insensitive. (Recall gave only 'Sensitivity of UTI: 90%'; stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: A teenage girl has lost a lot of weight by restricting food and exercising excessively, and has amenorrhoea and bradycardia. Thyroid function (TSH) is checked to exclude another cause. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Restriction, fear of weight gain, amenorrhoea and bradycardia point to anorexia nervosa. TFTs are part of the work-up to exclude hyperthyroidism. (Recall: 'anorexia nervosa scenario, diagnosis (TSH)'; stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: Same scenario (anorexia nervosa). On starting refeeding, which complication must be monitored most closely?
questions.exp: Refeeding syndrome: insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark and can cause heart failure, arrhythmia and seizures.

questions.question: A child with known congenital adrenal hyperplasia presents with hyperkalaemia. What is the most serious ECG sign?
questions.exp: Progression in hyperkalaemia: peaked T → prolonged PR and flattened P → wide QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole. A sine wave is pre-arrest.

questions.question: A child presents 8 hours after a paracetamol overdose. What do you do?
questions.a: Take a paracetamol level and start N-acetylcysteine without waiting for the result
questions.b: Wait for the level, then decide on treatment
questions.exp: At 8 hours or later, NAC efficacy falls with delay, so start it straight away after taking the level (when a significant dose is possible), then review against the treatment line.

questions.question: Which of the following shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the LEFT?
questions.exp: HbF binds 2,3-DPG poorly, so it has a higher oxygen affinity (left shift). Acidosis, raised CO2, fever and raised 2,3-DPG shift the curve right.

questions.question: A child has lower limb weakness after a URTI, with loss of sensation; reflexes are preserved. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A sensory level with bladder involvement and weakness after infection suggests transverse myelitis (reflexes may be preserved or brisk). GBS has areflexia with relatively preserved sensation.

questions.question: A child has lower limb weakness 1 month after a URTI. Reflexes are absent and sensation is preserved. Which investigation do you do?
questions.exp: Guillain–Barré syndrome: LP shows raised CSF protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation). Nerve conduction studies also support the diagnosis.

questions.question: A teenager took cocaine at a party and has been ventilated for 2 weeks. Death is confirmed. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: This is most likely death diagnosed by neurological (brain-stem) criteria
questions.b: Ventilation must continue until cardiac arrest before death can be confirmed
questions.c: This is a persistent vegetative state
questions.d: Death cannot be confirmed while the patient is on a ventilator
questions.exp: Death can be diagnosed by neurological criteria (brain-stem death testing by two senior doctors) while the heart beats on the ventilator. (Recall gave only the answer; options reconstructed.)

questions.question: Doctors performed CPR for 30 minutes and then decided to stop. The parents were unhappy and continued CPR themselves. Which ethical principle guided the doctors' decision?
questions.exp: Stopping futile resuscitation is a best-interests decision (beneficence and non-maleficence). The parents' wishes relate to autonomy, but they cannot oblige doctors to give futile treatment. The recall marked beneficence, with autonomy as a second choice.

questions.question: A child develops motor and vocal tics after his grandfather's death. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic for more than a year = Tourette syndrome; stress often worsens tics.

questions.question: A 26-week preterm baby received surfactant. Which of the following is NOT prevented by surfactant?
questions.exp: Surfactant reduces RDS severity, air leak and mortality but does not reduce IVH (antenatal steroids do).

questions.question: A newborn has cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, microphthalmia and a scalp defect. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Patau syndrome: midline defects (holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate), microphthalmia, post-axial polydactyly and aplasia cutis of the scalp. (Recall gave only the topic; stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: What is the most common complication of Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)?
questions.exp: Renal involvement, mostly microscopic haematuria, occurs in a third to a half of children; follow up with urinalysis and BP for 6–12 months. Intussusception is rarer (ileo-ileal).

questions.question: A newborn has a well-demarcated, hairless, membranous defect on the scalp vertex. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Aplasia cutis congenita: absent skin, usually at the vertex. A surrounding 'hair collar' suggests underlying neural tube or ectopic tissue. Naevus sebaceous is a yellow-orange, waxy hairless plaque. (Recall: 'cutis aplasia, presence of naevus'; stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: Regarding infantile spasms (West syndrome), which statement is correct?
questions.a: Tuberous sclerosis is a common cause, and vigabatrin is first-line in it
questions.c: Onset is typically after 2 years of age
questions.d: Untreated phenylketonuria is never a cause
questions.exp: West syndrome: spasms, hypsarrhythmia and developmental regression, onset 3–12 months. Causes include TSC, HIE, Down syndrome and metabolic disease (including untreated PKU). (The recalled item was unclear; options reconstructed.)

questions.question: A neonate with meningitis has an erythematous (granulomatous) rash and hepatosplenomegaly. Which organism is most likely?
questions.exp: Listeria (granulomatosis infantiseptica): sepsis/meningitis with a papular or granulomatous rash and hepatosplenomegaly; it is resistant to cephalosporins, so amoxicillin is added. (The recall was uncertain; stem reconstructed.)

questions.question: What is the diagnostic test for congenital CMV infection?
questions.a: Urine (or saliva) CMV PCR within the first 3 weeks of life, plus a hearing assessment
questions.exp: Congenital CMV is confirmed by PCR on urine or saliva taken within 21 days of birth; later samples cannot separate congenital from postnatal infection. Sensorineural hearing loss is the commonest sequela.

questions.question: Which test is used for newborn hearing screening?
questions.exp: Well babies are first screened with automated OAE; AABR is used when OAE fails and for NICU babies (to detect auditory neuropathy).

questions.question: A child who drinks excessive cow's milk presents with iron-deficiency anaemia. What is your advice?
questions.a: Reduce milk to under about 500 mL a day, give an iron supplement and refer to a dietitian
questions.exp: Excess cow's milk is low in iron, displaces iron-rich food and can cause occult GI blood loss. Limit milk, treat with oral iron for 3 months after Hb normalises, and give dietary advice.

questions.question: A neonate has a persistent red rash including the skin folds that has not responded to treatment. What is the next step?
questions.exp: The recall gave a low-potency topical steroid, which fits seborrhoeic or irritant dermatitis. If the rash is in the nappy area with satellite papules and the folds involved, think of candida and treat with a topical antifungal; read the stem carefully.

questions.question: Which is a side effect of amitriptyline?
questions.exp: Tricyclic side effects: sedation, dizziness (postural hypotension), anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention), tachycardia and QT prolongation.

questions.question: Bronchiolitis is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: RSV bronchiolitis causes neutrophil-predominant inflammation, epithelial necrosis and mucus plugging with air trapping. Eosinophilic inflammation is typical of asthma.

questions.question: A child presents with high fever, low blood pressure and delayed capillary refill. What is your approach?
questions.a: IV fluid bolus, IV antibiotics within the hour, and inotropes if shock persists
questions.d: Wait for blood cultures before antibiotics
questions.exp: Septic shock: 10 mL/kg crystalloid boluses with reassessment, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and early inotropes (adrenaline/noradrenaline) for fluid-refractory shock.

questions.question: In a child with septic shock, which of the following is NOT one of the 2-hour prognostic factors?
questions.exp: Response at 2 hours is judged on lactate, heart rate, blood pressure, perfusion and conscious level; the white cell count is not a marker of response.

questions.question: A neonate had antenatally diagnosed hydronephrosis. Which investigation is LEAST useful initially?
questions.exp: Postnatal work-up starts with ultrasound (after 48 hours), with MCUG if there is significant dilatation or suspected posterior urethral valves. DMSA looks for scarring/function later and is not an early test.

questions.question: The mother had rubella in pregnancy. Which congenital heart defect is most associated?
questions.exp: Congenital rubella: PDA and peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, with cataracts and sensorineural deafness.

questions.question: A 4-year-old has anaphylaxis. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Resuscitation Council UK: IM adrenaline 1:1000 — 150 micrograms under 6 years, 300 micrograms 6–12 years, 500 micrograms over 12. Antihistamines are not first-line.

questions.question: In incontinentia pigmenti, which cell is primarily affected?
questions.exp: The NEMO (IKBKG) mutation makes keratinocytes apoptose; melanin then 'drops' from the damaged basal epidermis into the dermis (pigment incontinence). Melanocytes themselves are normal. The recall marked melanocyte, so be aware of the alternative key.

questions.question: A teenage girl is a sports fan, eats healthy food and goes to the gym 4 times a week. TSH is slightly elevated and T4 is at the lower limit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: RED-S: low energy availability relative to exercise causes hormonal changes (low-normal T4/T3, menstrual disturbance, low bone density) without the body-image disturbance of anorexia nervosa.

questions.question: You are doing a study and an adolescent wants to take part without his parents' agreement. At what age can a minor give consent to take part in a non-investigational study?
questions.exp: The recall answer is 18, the age of majority in the UAE (DOH Abu Dhabi). In UK guidance, young people aged 16–17 can consent to non-drug (non-CTIMP) research.

questions.question: A 10-year-old has acute loss of vision in one eye; the retina shows a granuloma. The mother keeps many cats at home. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A unilateral retinal granuloma in an older child exposed to cats or dogs is ocular toxocariasis (Toxocara cati/canis). Ocular toxoplasmosis gives a retinochoroiditis scar with active satellite lesions. The recall marked both.

questions.question: A preterm baby in NICU was well, then suddenly deteriorates with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting and blood in the stool. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: NEC: preterm, enterally fed, sudden distension, bilious aspirates and bloody stool; X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. (Recall gave only the answer; options reconstructed.)

questions.question: A 4-year-old has fever, an evanescent rash, joint stiffness, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Systemic JIA: quotidian spiking fever, salmon-pink evanescent rash, arthritis, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and serositis. Exclude leukaemia (bone marrow) before steroids.

questions.question: A child falls and has pain and swelling of the lower limb; X-ray shows a Salter–Harris type 1 fracture. Which is correct about management?
questions.b: Salter–Harris type 1: treat with a cast
questions.exp: Type 1 (through the physis) fractures usually heal well with immobilisation in a cast; X-ray may look normal, so treat clinically.

questions.question: A jaundiced neonate is unwell with seizures and encephalopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy, hypotonia then hypertonia, retrocollis/opisthotonus and seizures. Treat with urgent exchange transfusion.
